summary: Defines TLS extensions that let a client and server agree to use OpenPGP certificates for authentication in a TLS session, and describes how to carry those certificates. It also creates a registry for non-X.509 certificate types. It is informational, not standards-track, and obsoletes RFC 5081.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a TLS connection authenticate with OpenPGP keys. A client sends a short list of the certificate types it can use, the server picks one, and the handshake then carries an OpenPGP key in place of the usual X.509 certificate. The extension is designed so that a client or server that only understands X.509 keeps working exactly as before.

subtitle: How a TLS client and server can agree to authenticate each other with OpenPGP keys instead of X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: TLS is defined around X.509 certificates, but the IETF also has a standard for OpenPGP certificates. A client whose key lives in OpenPGP had no way to use it to authenticate itself in a TLS session.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a TLS extension, cert_type with the value 9, that carries the certificate types each side supports and the one that was chosen, and it defines how an OpenPGP certificate is carried in the certificate messages of the handshake.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 5081, with which it is not backward-compatible. Existing clients and servers that use X.509 certificates are unaffected.

facts.value: empty_cert is 1, subkey_cert is 2, subkey_cert_fingerprint is 3

facts.value: 2 to 223 assigned via RFC Required, 224 to 255 reserved for Private Use

today: RFC 6091 was published in February 2011 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 5081, the earlier version of this work, with which it is not backward-compatible. It has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Why OpenPGP Keys in TLS
sections.content:
The IETF has two sets of standards for public key certificates: one for X.509 certificates and one for OpenPGP certificates. At the time of writing, the TLS standards are defined to use X.509 certificates. This document specifies a way to negotiate the use of OpenPGP certificates for a TLS session, and how to transport OpenPGP certificates over TLS.

The proposed extensions are backward-compatible with the TLS specification, so existing client and server implementations that use X.509 certificates are not affected. They are not backward-compatible with RFC 5081, the earlier version of this work, and the major differences are listed in Appendix A of the RFC. The OpenPGP CertificateType value is reused with the same number as in RFC 5081 but with different semantics, and the RFC argues that this causes no interoperability problem because the earlier document was not widely deployed.

On terminology, the RFC uses the term OpenPGP key as the OpenPGP specification does, and uses OpenPGP certificate to mean an OpenPGP key that is enabled for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS expects an X.509 certificate, but some people keep their key in OpenPGP instead of forcing it into a certificate authority's format. This RFC lets the two sides of a TLS connection say which kind of key they hold and agree on one, without disturbing anyone who only has X.509 certificates.

sections.title: The cert_type Extension
sections.content:
To indicate support for more than one certificate type, clients MUST include an extension of type cert_type in the extended client hello message. The extension is assigned the value 9 from the TLS ExtensionType registry, and the same number is used in both the client hello and the server hello.

The extension carries a list of the certificate types the client can use, sorted by client preference. It MUST be omitted if the client supports only X.509 certificates. Its data field holds a CertificateTypeExtension structure, which is used by both the client and the server even though it is specified once. The structure holds either a list of certificate types, in the client case, or a single certificate type, in the server case. The CertificateType enumeration defines X.509 as 0, OpenPGP as 1, and leaves 255 open.

No new cipher suites are needed to use OpenPGP certificates. Any existing cipher suite that supports a key exchange method compatible with the key in the certificate can be used with an OpenPGP certificate.

If the server receives a client hello containing the cert_type extension and chooses a cipher suite that requires a certificate, then two outcomes are possible. The server MUST either select a certificate type from the list in the extended client hello, or terminate the session with a fatal alert of type unsupported_certificate. The type the server selected is carried in a CertificateTypeExtension structure in the extended server hello message, using an extension of type cert_type. Servers that support only X.509 certificates MAY omit the extension from the server hello.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says which kinds of certificate it can offer, best first, in a short extra field in its first message. The server picks one and says so in the same field of its reply. If the server cannot use any of them, it ends the connection with a clear error rather than carrying on.

sections.title: Carrying an OpenPGP Certificate
sections.content:
The contents of the certificate message sent from server to client, and the other way round, are determined by the negotiated certificate type and by the key exchange algorithm of the selected cipher suite. If OpenPGP is negotiated, an OpenPGP certificate must be presented, and it must contain a public key that matches the selected key exchange algorithm: an RSA public key that can be used for encryption for the RSA key exchange, a DSA public key that can be used for authentication for DHE_DSS, and an RSA public key that can be used for authentication for DHE_RSA.

An OpenPGP certificate in the certificate message is sent using the binary OpenPGP format, and it must contain all the elements required by Section 11.1 of the OpenPGP specification. It is placed in the Certificate structure and tagged with the OpenPGPCertDescriptorType subkey_cert. Because such a certificate may hold several subkeys, the subkey to use for this session is named explicitly in the OpenPGPKeyID field. The key ID must be given even if the certificate has only a primary key. On receiving it, the peer must either use the named subkey or end the session with a fatal alert of unsupported_certificate.

There is a second option: send an OpenPGP fingerprint instead of the whole certificate, using the subkey_cert_fingerprint tag. That structure requires the primary key fingerprint as well as the subkey ID to use for the session. The peer answers with a certificate_unobtainable fatal alert if it cannot find a certificate with that fingerprint.

The descriptor types are empty_cert with the value 1, subkey_cert with the value 2 and subkey_cert_fingerprint with the value 3. The empty certificate uses a 24-bit value of zero. The subkey certificate structure holds a key ID of 8 to 255 bytes and a certificate of 0 to 2^24-1 bytes; the fingerprint structure holds a key ID of 8 to 255 bytes and a fingerprint of 20 to 255 bytes. Implementations MUST ensure that the sizes of key IDs and fingerprints comply with the OpenPGP specification, and it is RECOMMENDED that the keys used with this protocol have the authentication flag, 0x20, set. The cert_fingerprint and cert types from RFC 5081 are not used and are marked obsolete; the empty_cert type has replaced cert as a backward-compatible way to specify an empty certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: An OpenPGP key can hold several subkeys, so the handshake has to say which one is being used, otherwise the two sides could disagree about who signed what. The certificate travels in the normal binary OpenPGP format. As an alternative, the sender can send only a fingerprint of the key, which is much shorter but then the other side has to already be able to look the key up.

sections.title: Certificate Requests and Client Certificates
sections.content:
The Certificate Request message keeps the semantics it has in the TLS specification. However, if that message is sent and the negotiated certificate type is OpenPGP, the certificate_authorities list MUST be empty, because OpenPGP keys are not issued by a named certificate authority.

The Client Certificate message is sent only in response to a certificate request, uses the same formatting as the server certificate message, and must also present a certificate matching the negotiated certificate type. If OpenPGP certificates have been selected and the client has no certificate available, it must send a certificate structure of type empty_cert containing an OpenPGPEmptyCert value. The server SHOULD then respond with a handshake_failure fatal alert if client authentication is required.

All the other handshake messages are identical to those in the TLS specification.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server asks the client to prove who it is, the list of acceptable certificate authorities has to be left empty for OpenPGP, because there is no such authority to name. A client with no OpenPGP key sends an explicitly empty certificate rather than nothing, so the server can tell the difference between a missing key and a refused request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of the TLS, TLS extension and OpenPGP specifications apply. Questions about using the web of trust, and about identity and certificate verification, are outside the scope of this document; the RFC treats them as issues to be handled by the application layer protocols.

The protocol for negotiating the certificate type works in the same way as cipher suite negotiation in the TLS specification, with the addition of default values when the extension is omitted. Since those omissions have a single meaning and the same protection is applied to the values as with cipher suites, the RFC concludes that the security properties of this negotiation are the same as those of cipher suite negotiation.

When OpenPGP fingerprints are used instead of full certificates, the discussion of client certificate URLs in the TLS extensions specification applies, especially when external servers are used to retrieve keys. There is one important difference: the client certificate URL extension allows identifying a certificate without including certificate hashes, but that is not possible in this protocol. A certificate that is not sent is always identified by its fingerprint, which is a cryptographic hash of the certificate.

The RFC also notes what an eavesdropper learns. When confidentiality is not available, an eavesdropper can see the number and the types of certificates the two parties hold, along with the contents of the certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing the kind of certificate works like choosing a cipher suite, and the RFC argues it is just as safe. Using a fingerprint instead of the whole key is the one place where the design is stricter than a similar TLS extension, because a fingerprint cannot be omitted.

sections.title: The Certificate Type Registry and the Changes from RFC 5081
sections.content:
The RFC uses the registry and the cert_type extension originally defined by RFC 5081, and existing IANA references have been updated to point to this document. The TLS Certificate Types registry is updated so that the values 0 for X.509 and 1 for OpenPGP are defined here, the values from 2 through 223 decimal inclusive are assigned via RFC Required, and the values from 224 through 255 decimal inclusive are reserved for Private Use.

Appendix A of the RFC lists the changes from RFC 5081. The major one is in the server certificate and client certificate messages, and it makes implementations of this protocol incompatible with those of RFC 5081. The change requires the subkey IDs used for TLS authentication to be marked explicitly in the handshake, and it was decided in order to place no limitation on the contents of the OpenPGP certificates that can be used with this protocol. RFC 5081 required that an OpenPGP key or subkey be marked with the authentication flag, so authentication would have failed if the flag was not set or if it was set in more than one subkey. The protocol in this RFC has no such limitation.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry of certificate types now says which numbers mean X.509 and which mean OpenPGP, and reserves the rest. The bigger change is about OpenPGP keys: this RFC no longer insists that a key carry a particular flag, and it always names the subkey used, which is what makes it incompatible with the earlier version of this work.

viz.caption: THE CERTIFICATE TYPE NEGOTIATION IN THE TLS HANDSHAKE

messages.label: CLIENT HELLO
messages.note: Carries the cert_type extension with the certificate types the client supports, in preference order.

messages.label: SERVER HELLO
messages.note: Carries the single certificate type the server chose, or the session ends with an unsupported_certificate alert.

messages.label: SERVER CERTIFICATE
messages.note: Carries the OpenPGP certificate in binary OpenPGP format, tagged subkey_cert, with the subkey ID named explicitly.

items.label: empty_cert
items.desc: An empty certificate, sent when OpenPGP was chosen and the client has no key to offer.

items.label: subkey_cert
items.desc: The whole OpenPGP certificate in binary OpenPGP format, with the subkey ID for the session named.

items.label: subkey_cert_fingerprint
items.desc: The fingerprint of the certificate instead of the certificate, with the primary key fingerprint and the subkey ID.
